column1: What is the eutectic composition and melting point of tin-lead solder?
column2: 63% tin / 37% lead by weight, melting at a single temperature of 183°C (lower than either pure constituent).

column1: Why do non-eutectic solder alloys exhibit a 'pasty range' and why is this problematic?
column2: Solid and liquid phases coexist across a temperature interval instead of transforming simultaneously, creating semi-solid slurries prone to cold joints and premature mechanical failure under vibration.

column1: State the Gibbs phase rule and its simplified form for a binary alloy system at constant pressure.
column2: F = C - P + 2 (general form); at constant atmospheric pressure, F = C - P + 1, where F = degrees of freedom, C = components, P = phases.

column1: Why do tin-based solders develop 'tin whiskers' over time?
column2: Tin's body-centered tetragonal crystal structure is anisotropic—the c-axis expands much more than the a-axis during thermal cycling, driving whisker growth.

column1: Rank the three heat transfer mechanisms in soldering by dominance and state when radiation becomes non-negligible.
column2: Conduction dominates (direct contact via phonon/electron transfer); convection is secondary (forced air in reflow ovens); radiation becomes significant above ~350°C.

column1: What is the 'thermal time constant' in a solder joint, and why does it differ between a thin wire and a large copper pad?
column2: It's the characteristic time for heat to flow from the iron tip through the joint to equilibrium. A thin wire reaches equilibrium in 3-5s; a 2oz copper pad on a 6-layer board (acting as a heat sink) may take 15-30s+ due to much greater thermal mass.

column1: Name the four thermal phases of a solder reflow profile and their approximate temperature roles.
column2: Ramp (ambient→liquidus), Soak (150-200°C, flux activates, oxides dissolve), Reflow (exceeds liquidus, e.g. 217°C SAC305, solder becomes fluid), Cool (solidification).

column1: What two copper-tin intermetallic compounds form during solder wetting, and which is formed first/faster?
column2: Cu₆Sn₅ (eta phase, forms rapidly, 1-3μm within seconds at peak temp) and Cu₃Sn (epsilon phase); eta phase forms first and faster.

column1: Why are intermetallic compounds (IMCs) described as a 'materials science paradox' in solder joints?
column2: The same diffusion process that creates the IMC bond (essential for mechanical strength) also produces a brittle layer that, if excessively thick, introduces fracture planes and degrades reliability.

column1: What is 'homologous temperature' and why does it explain why solder creeps under sustained load at room temperature?
column2: Homologous temperature is the ratio of operating temperature to absolute melting temperature. Tin-based solders operate at ~0.6-0.7 of their homologous temperature at room temp, placing them in the creep regime, causing time-dependent plastic deformation under sustained stress.

column1: Compare the typical resistance of a good SMD solder joint versus a cold/marginal joint.
column2: Good joint: 1-10 mΩ. Marginal/cold joint: 50-500 mΩ or worse, due to voids and oxidation creating current constriction paths.

column1: Describe the self-reinforcing failure loop linking electrical resistance, heat, and IMC growth in a degrading solder joint.
column2: High resistance → Joule heating (P=I²R) → raises local temperature → accelerates diffusion/IMC growth → IMC layer thickens and becomes brittle → cracks form under thermal cycling → fracture causes intermittent faults under vibration/thermal transients.
